item.title: Why Starting Feels Harder Than Doing
item.description:
Procrastination

Why Starting Feels Harder Than Doing

How personality shapes procrastination and what you can do about it.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination can reflect low conscientiousness, high neuroticism, or both.
  • Avoiding a task provides immediate relief, reinforcing the urge to put it off.
  • Starting with a laughably small goal can challenge your predictions about the task.

Have you ever put off a task for weeks, only to discover that it took you just 15 minutes when you finally sat down to do it? In addition to procrastinating on big, complicated projects, many of us also put off smaller tasks like scheduling an appointment, responding to an email, filling out a form, or making a phone call. Seeing these tasks on your to-do list is almost guaranteed to make you feel guilty, but that still doesn’t seem to get you started.

Then, when you finally do the task, you feel silly that it caused so much angst since it only took a few minutes to complete. In fact, many of the things we put off aren’t terribly difficult. So, why do we have so much trouble getting started?

Before we begin, we're responding to what we expect the task will feel like. We imagine it will be tedious or take forever. We might be concerned that it will be frustrating, anxiety-provoking, or even overwhelming. And as long as we keep putting it off, we never get the information that proves our prediction wrong. Moreover, avoiding the task provides immediate relief, making us even more likely to put it off the next time.

The Personality Traits Behind Procrastination

People lower in conscientiousness may put off tasks because planning doesn't come naturally to them. They may have trouble estimating how long a task will take or breaking it into manageable steps. This makes relatively simple tasks feel bigger than they are and, without a clear sense of where to start or how long they'll need, it's easy to decide to tackle it later when the timing feels better.

For people higher in neuroticism, procrastination may have more to do with avoiding uncomfortable emotions. Thinking about making a phone call might make them feel self-conscious, booking a doctor’s appointment may bring up distressing thoughts about their health, and responding to emails may feel overwhelming. Putting these tasks off provides immediate relief from uncomfortable feelings, which is why we keep doing it even when we know procrastination rarely works out well in the long run.

Of course, these processes can overlap. You can be bad at estimating how long a task will take and feel anxious about doing it. Fortunately, regardless of which personality pattern is driving your procrastination, the path forward starts in the same place.

Make the Goal Laughably Small

When you find yourself putting something off, change the goal. Instead of telling yourself you have to finish a task, set a laughably manageable objective. For example, when my clients are struggling with procrastination, I tell them to set a timer for five minutes and just begin: Work on the presentation, start filling out the form, or open the email and start typing a response. If the timer goes off and the task really is as tedious, overwhelming, or uncomfortable as they imagined, they have my permission to stop.

In my experience, the result is usually anticlimactic. Sometimes people finish the task before the timer even goes off. Other times, they realize after five minutes of working that continuing doesn't seem nearly as difficult. Either way, they've collected evidence that the anticipation of doing the task was worse than actually doing it.

With repetition, these small experiments can challenge both paths to procrastination. You get better at judging how much time tasks actually require, while also learning that you can tolerate whatever discomfort comes with doing them.

Procrastination Doesn't Have to Be Your Personality

When you have a history of putting things off, it is easy to assume that you’re “just a procrastinator.” But personality traits are simply labels that summarize how you’ve behaved in the past, not how you’re destined to behave in the future.

One five-minute experiment isn't going to transform your personality. But repeated often enough, those small departures from your usual behavior begin to add up. Eventually, "I'm someone who always puts things off" may no longer feel like such an accurate description of who you are.

item.title: Why Smart People Learn but Still Don’t Change
item.description:
Education

Why Smart People Learn but Still Don’t Change

The hidden psychology that explains why insight rarely becomes behaviour.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Learning can feel threatening, even when we consciously want to change.
  • New ideas are harder to accept when they challenge our existing identity and beliefs.
  • Curiosity and psychological safety make behavioural change more likely than persuasion or pressure.
  • Lasting change rarely happens alone; managers, mentors and others help turn insight into action.

Smart leaders don't fail to learn through lack of will. They fail because no one taught them to notice the moment their brain quietly vetoes the idea before they've consciously considered it. -Dr Lynda Shaw, author of Off-Piste Thinking: Why Smart Leaders Make Bad Decisions

Source: Andy Lopata

We have never had easier access to ideas that promise to help us grow. Books, podcasts, keynote talks, online courses, and articles constantly offer new ways of thinking.

Yet how many people make meaningful behavioural changes after taking up these learning opportunities? Research consistently shows that turning insight into sustained behavioural change is far harder than most of us imagine.

It’s easy to assume that people don’t change because they lack motivation, discipline or commitment. Or that time is the barrier—once we return to our desks after a training course or conference, switch off a podcast or put our book down, real life simply gets in the way of applying and embedding what we have learned.

Some of this may be true, but it’s not the whole picture. The real barrier may lie in our brains doing exactly what they evolved to do.

Your Brain Thinks Learning Is Risky

There’s a familiar awkwardness you may recognise in any learning scenario. The facilitator has presented an idea and asked the group for their thoughts or questions. However experienced and senior the group, the response is typically the same—nervous silence as everyone waits for someone else to speak.

Why do capable and often powerful professionals suddenly become so hesitant in this situation?

Katie Swandale, an education behaviour specialist and senior learning and development leader, believes the answer lies in our natural response to danger. Swandale explained, “The brain isn't trying to embarrass you or keep you locked in that way. It's just trying to protect you. For many, school spent years training patterns of social stakes around learning, which the brain keeps encoded into adulthood—and our brains genuinely struggle to distinguish between social and physical threats.”

David Rock’s SCARF model, which shows how our brain detects reward or threat triggers and responds accordingly, helps explain why. When our existing understanding is challenged, the brain often interprets uncertainty as a threat rather than opportunity. Instead of new ideas sparking curiosity, we seek to withdraw and protect ourselves.

For learning to be applied, it’s important for us to override this neural response and create a trusted learning environment. Fear of failure has long been recognised as an obstacle to learning. Swandale's observation suggests something even more fundamental: for many of us, the threat response begins before we've even had the chance to fail.

Adults Don’t Reject Ideas, They Protect Identities

One of the biggest reasons new learning can feel like a threat is that it challenges the identity already in place. Adults don’t arrive as blank pages; we arrive with a full script already written, shaped by years of experience, habits reinforced by positive results, strong beliefs and a clear identity.

When a new idea challenges that identity, we’re no longer evaluating information; we’re defending ourselves.

Therefore, we may have to start questioning some of our deeply ingrained assumptions if we are going to be able to take new ideas on board.

According to Swandale, "The brain feels safer arriving at new insight itself and processing it with previous experiences. The moment it feels like someone is trying to change your mind, you start defending the mind you already have.

“But there is still a place for learning and development in this scenario—we don’t need to control the outcome in its entirety, instead we can give nudges and learning opportunities to help people arrive at a conclusion that feels truthful to them."

Perhaps this is why curiosity changes minds far more effectively than persuasion. And that’s why the source of the information counts, and the trust referenced earlier is so important. If our identity and beliefs are to be challenged, we are more likely to respond positively if we implicitly trust the person or organisation presenting that challenge.

Insight Doesn’t Change Behaviour, Relationships Do

Understanding the problem points us towards the solution. Insight matters, but insight alone rarely changes behaviour. We need to recognise the natural obstacles to progress and work to overcome them so that insights land and are acted upon.

Lasting change happens when someone helps us make sense of what we've learned, encourages us to apply it, and checks in afterwards. As Swandale points out, “Learning without accountability is like throwing a seed into soil and never watering it. The training isn't necessarily the problem. The conditions for growth simply aren't there."

The CIPD Learning at Work Survey in 2023 found that only 36% of line managers actively support their teams in applied learning. If you send people off to have their practices, ideas, and even identities challenged, you can’t be surprised if, without support, they don’t come back transformed.

In the workplace, we need a culture that encourages and revisits learning. Managers, coaches, and mentors can play a key role here. "Managers don't need to be experts in the content”, according to Swandale. “They simply need to be curious. Someone caring and actively discussing whether the learning lands fundamentally changes how people engage with it."

Behaviour rarely changes in isolation. It changes because people are curious about what they’ve learned, notice their progress, feel emboldened, and create the space to experiment with new approaches.

Perhaps we have spent too long trying to improve learning experiences rather than improving the conditions surrounding them.

Insight matters, but insight isn’t enough. People change when they feel psychologically safe, when their identity isn't under attack, when curiosity and exploration replace judgment, and when someone continues the conversation long after the initial moment of learning has passed.

Perhaps learning doesn't really happen when we encounter a new idea. Perhaps it happens in the conversations that help us make sense of it afterwards.

item.title: Why We Should Talk to Our Family Elders
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Why We Should Talk to Our Family Elders

A Personal Perspective: Who we come from plays an important role in who we are.

Posted August 24, 2026

One of the books I have written is called The Spoon from Minkowitz, about the tiny village my grandmother came from in what is today Ukraine. Growing up, I repeatedly asked my grandmother for details about her life, but, like many immigrants, she didn’t want to talk about what she left behind. Over many years, I extracted six facts from her, like what the floor of her house was made of, that she dried tobacco leaves with the women when she was 10, that she wasn’t allowed to go to school, and that she admired the girls who got educated and wore uniforms.

When I finally went to the village, I wept from the moment I arrived until the time I left. I found the six clues, thanks to the mayor who helped me. I felt connected to those who came before me as I walked the dirt road they walked on, breathed the air they breathed, ate some of the foods they once ate. I became convinced that to really know who we are and to feel whole, we have to know what came before us. Even if we know nothing about them, they had an enormous impact on our lives, and we wouldn’t be here without them.

When I gave talks about the book, many members of the audience wept. They came up to me afterwards and said they wished they had asked their grandparents and other relatives about their lives. In many cases, they felt it was too late as their ancestors were gone, their memories had faded, and there was no one left to ask. One woman cried and said, “I don’t feel whole. I feel a tree or a plant that has no roots. You need roots to be nourished and grow.”

An important article on the subject reveals that “research from the Legacy Project shows that while 94% of seniors would be happy to share their life stories, only 32% have actually been asked by their families—and even when asked, many elderly parents remain reluctant to open up about their experiences.”

In addition to providing stories about your family, the article reveals other benefits of talking to elders. “The Legacy Project, particularly Cornell University’s initiative led by Dr. Karl Pillemer, gathers practical, "on-the-ground" advice from over 1,200 Americans in their 80s, 90s, and 100s, focusing on life lessons. These seniors share wisdom on marriage, child-rearing, aging, and career to help younger generations avoid regrets. Key lessons include prioritizing happiness, living in the moment, and staying connected.”

In my experience, I have found that it’s best to ease into a conversation, rather than plunging headlong into questions about their emotional, psychological lives and relationships. If there was intergenerational trauma, you may opt to begin with other, easier aspects of life first. You may, for example, ask what their favorite foods were, or how certain holidays were celebrated. You can inquire about their favorite item of clothing, or if they had a pet. If you are patient, you will get to deeper questions, or maybe you’ll be satisfied with just learning about simple things.

I always carry with me a little 3 x 5 notebook, and I often ask if I may write down their answers. “I want to remember everything you are saying,” I comment, “and would it be okay with you if I record it so I don’t forget it?” Some elders agree to be recorded and photographed if they feel you are genuinely interested in them. The most important thing is to relax and move slowly, so they don’t feel rushed. The ideal situation is that you feel connected to each other, and the information flows freely and comfortably.

It is wonderful to live in the present, but it can be very meaningful to dive into the past when it involves learning about what and who came before us, and how that contributes to our sense of knowing who we are, and on whose shoulders we stand in our current lives.
